owner_instruction: Ahmed instructed this go-live on 9 Oct 2026 after being told the letter reads as AI-drafted and the returned forms were blank.

paediatrics_held_01.note: PAAKT183 and PAQ977 are Held 01 items; the letter lists their edits under Pack 3 (H01).

retired.reason: PED002 is the same scenario: prolonged jaundice with pale stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly in a 5-6 week old, with urgent referral as the answer and reassurance or breast milk jaundice as distractors (BX909 gives biliary atresia as the diagnosis). The held item adds nothing.

HAE010 is the same scenario: a preschool child with pallor, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, cytopenias and blasts on film, with ALL as the answer. The held item's options are mainly a choice between diagnoses with the obvious same-day referral attached.

PED009 is the same scenario: a toddler with a brief generalised febrile seizure from otitis media who recovers fully, with observation and discharge with safety-netting as the answer (simple febrile seizure).
PED021 tests the same learning point: methylphenidate is first-line medication for ADHD in children. The held item only adds that environmental measures were tried first.
PED029 tests the same fact: placing the baby on their back to sleep is the single most important way to reduce the risk of SIDS.

DT029 and PED038 are the same scenario: an infant with bilateral subdural and retinal haemorrhages and an inadequate history, with an urgent safeguarding referral to children's social care as the answer.
BX256 is the same infant with paroxysmal crying, knees drawn up and blood-and-mucus stool, asking the diagnosis of intussusception. Same scenario and learning point.
BX104 is a young infant with projectile non-bilious vomiting who feeds hungrily afterwards, asking the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. Same scenario and diagnosis; the palpable olive adds little.
BX105 is a school-age child with stereotyped self-limiting vomiting episodes and wellness in between, keyed cyclical vomiting syndrome. Same scenario and diagnosis.

PED009 is a toddler fully recovered from a brief febrile generalised seizure, keyed discharge with safety-netting. Same scenario and management; the held item frames it as advice to the parent (call 999 if over 5 minutes).
PED023 is an infant with several days of high fever and a blanching truncal rash appearing as the fever settles, keyed roseola infantum. Same scenario and diagnosis.
PED049 is a young child with fever, mouth ulcers and palm/sole vesicles, keyed supportive care because it is self-limiting. Same scenario and management decision.
BX192 and PED041 are infants with mild bronchiolitis, adequate feeding and acceptable saturations, keyed supportive care. Same scenario and management decision.
PED007 and PED047 are mild croup with barking cough and stridor only when upset, keyed a single dose of oral dexamethasone. Same scenario and treatment.
PAAKT135 includes resuscitation and informing the surgical team; better distractors.
PED048 is jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours, keyed urgent investigation because it is always pathological. Same scenario and decision (urgent bilirubin and look for a cause).
PED046 is a non-mobile infant with a spiral long-bone fracture and an inconsistent, changing history, keyed admit, treat the fracture and make a safeguarding referral. Same scenario and action.
PED026 is an unstable hip on Ortolani testing, keyed ultrasound of the hips. The held item is the same abnormal hip examination and investigation, at the newborn check rather than 6 weeks.
PED012 is a febrile young child with leucocytes and nitrites on dipstick, keyed send urine for culture and start empirical oral antibiotics. Same scenario and management decision.
PED033 is a young child with hard stools, overflow soiling and a palpable faecal mass, keyed macrogol at disimpaction dose. Same scenario and treatment.
PAPAED188 states there is no DKA and has stronger distractors.

NEU100 is suspected meningococcal disease with a non-blanching rash seen in primary care, keyed immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin and urgent transfer. Same learning point; the held patient is a child on a home visit with septicaemia rather than a young adult with meningitis.

PED025 is an unvaccinated infant with paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting, keyed pertussis treated with azithromycin; ID003 covers contact prophylaxis. The held item adds notification but the core learning point (macrolide for infant pertussis) is the same.
PED022 is a child with sore throat, sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue and circumoral pallor, keyed group A strep treated with penicillin V. Same scenario and treatment; notification is an add-on.
BX945 and BX380 are a child with fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a descending rash, keyed measles. Same scenario and diagnosis.
BX382 is bilateral painful parotid swelling keyed mumps and BX774 is mumps orchitis as the complication; the held item combines these same two recall facts.
PED058 and BX067 are a well, afebrile child with a limp after a viral illness and normal markers, keyed transient synovitis. Same scenario and diagnosis.
BX062 is a young boy with a limp over weeks and restricted hip internal rotation, keyed Perthes disease. Same scenario and diagnosis; the X-ray findings add little.
S033 is a boy with a testis not palpable in the scrotum or groin, keyed referral to paediatric urology for surgery. Same scenario and management decision.
BX117 is a 2-year-old choking while eating then with unilateral right-sided wheeze, keyed foreign body aspiration. Same scenario and diagnosis.
PED020 is a toddler with poor eye contact, no pointing, absent speech and repetitive behaviour, keyed referral for autism diagnostic assessment. Same scenario and decision.

BX773 is a pregnant contact of rubella keyed risk of congenital rubella syndrome, which is the held item's key concern; the held item also requires recognising rubella from the child's rash and occipital nodes.
BX1127 is a short adolescent girl with primary amenorrhoea, absent breast development and short fourth metacarpals, keyed Turner syndrome. Same scenario and diagnosis; prescreen flag confirmed.
PED009 is a toddler recovered from a brief febrile seizure with a red bulging eardrum, keyed observe then discharge with safety-netting. Same scenario and management decision.

P055 is the same school-age child with over a year of hyperactivity and inattention at home and school, answered by specialist referral; the held item asks the same next step for suspected ADHD, though the P055 key also bundles parent training.
BX494 tests the same fact: ADHD symptoms must be present in more than one setting; the held item tests the pervasiveness criterion in the reverse direction (school-only symptoms).
PED011 is a child with fever, non-blanching purpuric rash and poor perfusion, answered by IV ceftriaxone now without awaiting investigations; same scenario and same immediate action.
PED043 is a well febrile toddler with all green features, managed at home with clear safety-netting; the held item adds an anxious parent but the key decision (reassure and safety-net) is the same.
PAQ1235 lists the traffic-light features in its own stem and has implausible distractors (Apgar, CURB-65).
Both test exploring vaccine concerns without coercion; PAAKT133 kept (borderline: the myths differ).
PAQ1152 has fuller severity signs and a chest X-ray distractor (close call).
PAAKT134 has a give-away distractor ("for scarlet fever") and the longest option as the key.
PED046 is a non-mobile 6-month-old with a femoral fracture, inconsistent history and multiple bruises, answered by admission and safeguarding referral; same scenario and same action.

BX104 is the same 5-week-old with projectile non-bilious vomiting, answered as pyloric stenosis, and PED014/DT033 cover the electrolytes and fluids; the held item combines diagnosis with management (fluids then pyloromyotomy) but the diagnostic point is the same.
PED054 is a very premature toddler with delayed walking, scissoring, increased tone and brisk reflexes answered as spastic cerebral palsy; same scenario and diagnosis.
BX911 is a 3-year-old with recurrent chest infections, poor weight gain and greasy stools answered as cystic fibrosis; same scenario and diagnosis.
PAQ14897 has the classic stridor-only-when-upset picture and the better explanation.
BX117 is a toddler with sudden choking and unilateral wheeze answered as foreign body aspiration; same scenario and diagnosis.
HAE008 is a 7-year-old with petechiae after a viral URTI and isolated thrombocytopenia, answered as ITP (with observation); same scenario and diagnosis.
PED048 is jaundice at 18 hours of age answered by urgent investigation because jaundice within 24 hours is pathological; same scenario and decision.
PED048 tests the same fact: jaundice within the first 24 hours is always pathological and needs urgent investigation.
CARD054 is a child with migratory polyarthritis, fever and a new murmur weeks after a sore throat answered as acute rheumatic fever; prescreen flag confirmed.
BX381 tests the same recognition: paroxysmal coughing bouts ending in an inspiratory whoop with post-tussive vomiting means pertussis; PED025 is the infant version.
BX357 is the same jittery, sleepy baby of a diabetic mother answered as hypoglycaemia must be excluded first; the held item asks for blood glucose as the first test, which is the same learning point.

Held PAQ16393 (labelled Infectious Diseases) is a 5-year-old nursery child with itchy papules, vesicles and crusts at different stages keyed chickenpox, the same diagnosis. Parked UN9623, UN8262, UN1842 and UN5955 are the same point too.
PED034 is a term infant with delayed meconium, abdominal distension and explosive stool on rectal exam answered as Hirschsprung disease (with biopsy); same scenario and diagnosis.
PAQ990 gives both low calcium and raised ALP and has the better explanation.
PED001 is a 2-day-old well, feeding term baby with face and chest jaundice answered as physiological jaundice; same scenario and diagnosis.
PED058 and BX067 are a well child limping a week after a viral illness answered as transient synovitis; same scenario and diagnosis.
BX594 is a febrile child refusing to bear weight with the hip held flexed, answered as septic arthritis must be excluded; same scenario and diagnosis.
BX909 is prolonged neonatal jaundice with pale stools answered as biliary atresia; same scenario and diagnosis (PED002 is the referral step).
PED032 and BX106 are school-age children with recurrent periumbilical pain, pallor and nausea, well between episodes, with family migraine, answered as abdominal migraine; prescreen flag confirmed.
BX105 is a school-age child with stereotyped episodes of intense vomiting lasting 1-2 days, well between, answered as cyclical vomiting syndrome; same scenario and diagnosis.
PAQ974 adds the urine dipstick finding and an HUS distractor (close call).

NEP011 and BX865 are young children with periorbital oedema, heavy proteinuria and low albumin asking for the underlying cause, keyed minimal change disease; PED051 is the same 3-year-old scenario. Same scenario and same diagnosis.

PED052, NEP050 and NEP010 all present a child with dark urine, periorbital oedema and hypertension weeks after a streptococcal infection (NEP050 explicitly includes skin infection), keyed post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Impetigo as the trigger does not change the learning point.

GAS027 is a child with bloody diarrhoea after a petting farm visit, reduced urine output and thrombocytopenia keyed haemolytic uraemic syndrome. The held item is the established-HUS version (diagnosis rather than complication to monitor), but the scenario and answer are the same.

BX261 is a schoolboy with cough and wheeze triggered by football keyed asthma, and BX912 keys asthma for wheeze with eczema and hay fever. The held item combines these features in a child and asks the same diagnosis; the prescreen flag is confirmed.

PED020 is a toddler who does not respond to his name, has few words, hand-flaps and does not point, asking for the next step, keyed referral for autism diagnostic assessment. Same scenario and same management decision.

DT042 is a preschool child with speech behind peers and recurrent winter colds keyed referral for hearing tests and tympanometry. The held item (sociable 30-month-old with isolated speech delay and ear infections) has the same decision, hearing assessment first, though DT042 adds otoscopy findings of OME.

PED017 (HSP, most important long-term monitoring: regular blood pressure and urinalysis) and DR153 (IgA vasculitis follow-up: serial urine dipsticks) have the same scenario and same monitoring decision. Missed by the prescreen.

PED015 is a 3-year-old with 6 days of fever and Kawasaki features asking for the most important complication to prevent, keyed coronary artery aneurysms; BX118 is the same. Same scenario and learning point.

BX775 is a child with fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes and no cough keyed acute bacterial tonsillitis; the held item uses the same Centor picture to ask the organism (Streptococcus pyogenes). Essentially the same fact, but the key is phrased differently, hence borderline.

PED025 is an unvaccinated young infant with paroxysmal cough, post-cough vomiting and apnoea keyed pertussis, and BX381 keys pertussis for paroxysmal cough. Same scenario and diagnosis; the antenatal vaccine and sibling details do not change the learning point.

BX115 is a child with chronic bowel symptoms asking which feature most suggests an organic cause, keyed faltering growth; BX530 is the adult equivalent keyed weight loss. Same decision and answer as the held item, though BX115's presenting complaint is constipation rather than pain with loose stools.

BX189 is a term newborn with immediate grunting, cyanosis, reduced left-sided breath sounds and a sunken abdomen keyed congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Same scenario and diagnosis; the prescreen flag is confirmed.

PAN3491 is an unimmunised small child with drooling, upright posture and soft stridor, keyed keep her calm with her parent and call 999. The held item is the ED version (keep calm with father, call senior anaesthetic and ENT help); the setting differs but the learning point (do not disturb, get airway experts) is the same.
S033 is a 1-year-old boy with a unilateral testis not palpable in the scrotum or inguinal canal, keyed refer to paediatric urology for surgery. Same scenario and management decision.
BX254 is a 29-week baby with grunting, nasal flaring and recession asking the underlying mechanism, keyed surfactant deficiency. Same scenario and answer; the prescreen flag is confirmed.

held_h01_paediatrics.note: None is named among the letter's H01 edits (PAQ932, PAAKT183, PAQ977) or rejects (PAN15778, PAQ932 conditional), and all four are approved in Held 01. The 2 approve / 1 edit / 1 reject split in the #66 record was inferred from counts and is not supported by the letter. The 6 H01 Paediatrics section-3 items (PAPAED169, 172, 174, 178, 182, 186) are among the 79 Held 01 retirements.

held_back_to_next_review_pack.reason: Approved in Paediatrics Batch 2, but it repeats PAQ300 (approved in Paediatrics Held 01, now live): same scenario and learning point. Held back so the two do not both go live; Ahmed or the reviewer to choose. The two were never reviewed side by side.

Approved in Paediatrics Batch 2, but it repeats PAQ15511 (approved in Paediatrics Held 01, now live): same scenario and learning point. Held back so the two do not both go live; Ahmed or the reviewer to choose. The two were never reviewed side by side.

Approved in Paediatrics Batch 2, but it repeats PAQ15553 (approved in Paediatrics Held 01, now live): same scenario and learning point. Held back so the two do not both go live; Ahmed or the reviewer to choose. The two were never reviewed side by side.

edits.before: She had her first MMR and other one-year vaccines eight days ago
edits.after: She had her first MMRV and other one-year vaccines eight days ago

edits.before: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine
edits.after: MMRV is a live attenuated vaccine

edits.before: as the vaccine virus replicates.
edits.after: as the vaccine virus replicates. MMRV can also cause a mild, spotty chickenpox-like rash, usually around the injection site 3 to 4 weeks after vaccination; unlike the measles-like rash, these spots may contain vaccine virus and should be kept covered.
edits.note: reviewer edit: add that MMRV can cause a mild varicella-like rash (NHS.uk MMRV vaccine, reviewed Dec 2025)

edits.before: chapter 21 Measles, 2013 (updated 2026).
edits.after: chapter 21 Measles, 2013 (updated 2026); NHS.uk MMRV vaccine, 2025.
edits.note: source for the added MMRV rash sentence

edits.before: The child is not infectious to others
edits.after: This measles-like rash is not infectious to others
edits.note: wording: makes clear the non-infectious statement is about this rash, not the later spots

edits.before: MMR Vaccine
edits.after: MMRV Vaccine
edits.note: consistency with the edited stem (shown to candidates as the learning objective)

edits.before: about a week after MMR in a well child
edits.after: about a week after MMRV in a well child

edits.before: a week after MMR in a well child
edits.after: a week after MMRV in a well child

edits.before: fever and rash after MMR suggest measles
edits.after: fever and rash after MMRV suggest measles

edits.before: Rubella — risk of congenital rubella syndrome affecting his mother's pregnancy
edits.after: Rubella — risk of congenital rubella syndrome

edits.before: Roseola infantum — risk of febrile seizures
edits.after: Roseola infantum — risk of febrile seizures during the high fever before the rash
edits.note: rebalance: after the D edit the key was the longest option; E lengthened with an accurate qualifier and no pregnancy or haemolysis cue

edits.before: Intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin now, with lumbar puncture once safe
edits.after: Intravenous ceftriaxone plus amoxicillin now, with lumbar puncture once safe

edits.before: E. Intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin now, with lumbar puncture once safe
edits.after: E. Intravenous ceftriaxone plus amoxicillin now, with lumbar puncture once safe

edits.before: Antibiotics must not be delayed: under 3 months, cefotaxime is combined with amoxicillin to cover Listeria, which cephalosporins miss.
edits.after: Antibiotics must not be delayed: give intravenous ceftriaxone (cefotaxime only if ceftriaxone is contraindicated), and under 3 months add amoxicillin to cover Listeria, which cephalosporins miss.

edits.before: Source: NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management, 2019 (updated 2021).
edits.after: Source: NICE NG240 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease: recognition, diagnosis and management, 2024 (recommendations 1.6.5 and 1.6.6); NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management, 2019 (updated 2021), recommendation 1.5.7 (Listeria cover under 3 months).
edits.note: source updated for the reviewer edit

edits.before: B. Ceftriaxone alone does not cover Listeria and cefotaxime is generally preferred in young infants.
edits.after: B. Ceftriaxone is the right cephalosporin, but on its own it does not cover Listeria, so amoxicillin must be added under 3 months.
edits.note: consistency: the old text said cefotaxime is preferred, which the reviewer edit reverses

edits.before: In infants under 3 months, add amoxicillin to the cephalosporin for Listeria.
edits.after: In infants under 3 months with suspected bacterial meningitis, give IV ceftriaxone (cefotaxime only if ceftriaxone is contraindicated) plus amoxicillin for Listeria.

edits.before: Intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin, lumbar puncture when safe
edits.after: Intravenous ceftriaxone plus amoxicillin, lumbar puncture when safe
edits.note: consistency with the new key text

edits.before: Suspected meningitis under 3 months: immediate IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin; do not delay for LP.
edits.after: Suspected meningitis under 3 months: immediate IV ceftriaxone plus amoxicillin (cefotaxime only if ceftriaxone is contraindicated); do not delay for LP.

edits.before: Source: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s, 2009.
edits.after: Source: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s, 2009, recommendation 1.3.3.2 (rapid intravenous infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride for shock); Advanced Paediatric Life Support (APLS), Advanced Life Support Group, for intraosseous access when intravenous access cannot be obtained quickly.

edits.before: Moderate
edits.after: Difficult

edits.before: Source: American Academy of Pediatrics, Atlantoaxial instability in children with Down syndrome.
edits.after: Source: Down Syndrome Medical Interest Group (DSMIG UK), Cervical spine disorders: craniovertebral instability, revised 2024.
edits.note: reviewer edit: UK source found (https://www.dsmig.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/CS-guide-final-10.10.2025.pdf; Box 1 warning signs include torticollis, neck pain, gait change and bladder change; Box 2 brisk reflexes and extensor plantars)

independent_check: Agent check of all 6 edited items and the other 114: 6 ok after one fix (PAQ15063 presentation and why_correct wording); no unlogged changes; the other 114 are identical to their reviewed versions apart from section.
